name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: An AI Gateway for Routing and Governing LLM Traffic
answer: LiteLLM is an AI gateway from BerriAI that gives one OpenAI-style interface to over 100 LLM APIs, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging. It began as a Python library and now ships a Rust core with a Python SDK, plus a proxy for production traffic. A reader deciding whether to adopt it should know that the project is mid-migration to Rust, so the Python proxy and the Rust gateway differ sharply in throughput and memory today.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and lives at github.com/BerriAI/litellm, with documentation at docs.litellm.ai. It is an AI gateway, meaning it sits between your application and the model providers rather than being a training framework or a model itself. The site describes it as the fastest, litest AI Gateway, a Rust core with a Python SDK, able to call more than 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging across providers such as Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM. The repository lists Python as its language, a custom licence, and roughly 60,078 stars, with a last push on 3 October 2026. It occupies the routing, governance and observability layer of the AI stack, the part that decides which model answers a request and records what that cost.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The documentation shows LiteLLM used for calling many providers through one interface, for reliability testing across providers, for load testing endpoints, and for production concerns such as SSO and SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management and guardrails. Its blog describes an Agent Gateway, a Model Gateway and an MCP Gateway forming one control plane, where the Agent Gateway authenticates callers and records request, response, latency and cost data, the Model Gateway routes LLM traffic and applies budgets and rate limits, and the MCP Gateway centralises tool access and upstream authentication. Budgets can be set at key, team, agent and customer level. It is strongest where a team needs one place to route traffic across providers, attribute spend per user or team, and enforce limits, rather than where raw model training or inference kernels are the concern.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is the gentler entry point, and the tutorials show short code examples such as batch_completion_models_all_responses and load_test_model, so a developer comfortable with Python can start without deep mathematics. The harder parts are operational rather than mathematical: running the proxy, understanding Redis behaviour, budgets, rate limits, routing and caching semantics. The site's own incident reports show how much provider-specific detail matters, for example that moving every role: system entry into a top-level system field on the Bedrock Invoke path broke Anthropic prompt caching. The official material offers tutorials, a blog and incident reports, but the facts here do not show a structured beginner curriculum, so a newcomer should expect to learn by reading documentation and examples rather than a guided course.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: LiteLLM connects to a wide set of providers, named in the site description as Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, and it speaks the A2A JSON-RPC interface for agent calls and works with MCP servers for tool access. It supports OIDC and other LiteLLM credentials for user authentication, and OAuth2 with the authorization_code flow for per-user MCP sign-in. The documentation includes tutorials, a blog with tags such as ai-gateway and incident-report, and an Admin UI where agents appear with status and spend data. The repository carries about 60,078 stars, which indicates a substantial community, and the blog mentions an early beta programme for the Rust gateway aimed at teams wanting to work directly with the maintainers. The facts do not give contributor counts, release cadence beyond specific versions, or third-party plugin listings.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LiteLLM serves both ends, but the two ends currently look different. The Python SDK and proxy are the quick path, and the site's own numbers show the cost: the Python proxy peaks around 359MB of memory under load, and per-request overhead is about 7.5ms on the Python path. The Rust gateway is the production-performance path, with the site claiming about 15x the throughput, 453 to 6,782 requests per second, on about 11x less memory, 359MB to 32MB, and per-request overhead near 0.05ms, well under the sub-1ms commitment. The site says the migration aims at a pure Rust server serving 100% of traffic, with hot paths such as auth and rate limiting in Rust, and that you deploy a single binary. The trade is maturity: the Rust gateway is described as an early beta, so teams wanting it accept a younger component in exchange for speed and memory control.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts show enterprise use rather than naming specific companies. An incident report describes an enterprise customer running litellm-database:v1.100.0 behind nginx with a proxy fleet in Kubernetes, and another describes customers running Claude Code against Amazon Bedrock through LiteLLM. The site mentions SSO and SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management and guardrails built for production, and a benchmark comparing the Rust gateway against Portkey, Bifrost and the Python proxy. That points to a current, actively developed tool rather than a legacy choice, and skills in gateway configuration, provider routing, budget and identity management transfer to platform and LLMOps roles. The facts do not include adoption surveys, customer counts or salary data, so claims about how widely it is used in any particular industry would go beyond what is supported here.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is written in Python with a Rust core, and the site frames it as a gateway that other code calls rather than a framework that owns your application. It is typically used alongside provider SDKs and APIs, which it calls directly over HTTP via httpx, and alongside MCP servers for tools and A2A for agent-to-agent calls. It sits in front of inference servers such as vLLM and hosted endpoints such as Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI and Nvidia NIM, so it belongs to the polyglot pattern where a Python application, a Rust gateway and provider-side services each do the part they are best at. The facts do not describe integrations with training frameworks such as PyTorch or with orchestration libraries, so its place beside those is not settled by the material here.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid about weaknesses. The Python proxy uses far more memory and adds more latency than the Rust gateway, and the Rust gateway is an early beta, so the fast path is not yet the default. The incident reports describe a Medium severity outage where retries plus an unreachable Redis produced unbounded memory growth, one worker reaching 61GB RSS, and a silent cost regression where Anthropic prompt caching broke and team daily spend rose 2-3x with requests still returning 200s. The licence is listed as custom, and the facts do not explain its terms. The site does not say when the Rust migration will finish, how the custom licence affects commercial use, or how the gateway compares on classification accuracy, since the site itself notes its router benchmark used synthetic prompts without independent review.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
